68_marg795: The apostle again writes this epistle to the Thessalonians. For a graver tribulation having arisen among them, he again admonishes them to patience, showing the just judgment of God, that the good may obtain glory, the wicked punishment. He also writes that the day of the Lord is not at hand, as it seemed to be on the occasion of the former epistle. For when, in reading the former epistle, they had come to that place where the Apostle says: “The dead shall rise first at his coming. Then we who are alive, who are left, shall be taken up together with them,” etc., they were troubled and exceedingly terrified, thinking the day of the Lord near, lest they should be condemned because, having come late to the faith, they were imperfect. And therefore, having learned this, he wrote to them that the day of judgment is not imminent, but will come in its own time, lest the apostle, having lied in this, should be rejected in everything, or lest the devil should mock those who await these things by some deceit. He also rebukes the restless more sharply.

Yet I say “just” on this condition: “If it be just with God,” etc. As if to say: the judgment by which God now judges appears just. If the future judgment be considered, where justice is manifest to all, when he renders to each according to merits, by which present things also are proved just, namely finally, if it is just to give these punishment and you rest: for whoever considers this end does not say it is unjust that the good are purified and the wicked grow foul, as each has deserved by his own life. David says something like this: “I studied that I might know this thing, it is a labour in my sight, until I go into the sanctuary of God, and understand concerning their last ends.” But yet it can be seen from present things; whence he adds: “But indeed for deceits thou hast put it to them: when they were lifted up thou hast cast them down,” etc.

And this which he said, “For the mystery of iniquity already worketh,” they wished to be understood of Nero, whose deeds seemed those of Antichrist; whence some suspected that he was either snatched away alive and hidden until he be revealed in his time, or that, having been slain, he would rise again and be the future Antichrist. And that it was said of this: “And now you know what withholdeth.” And when he says, “only that he who now holdeth, do hold,” they say the apostle exhorts the faithful to persevere steadfastly in the faith which they hold, until the mystery of iniquity, which is now hidden, go out of the midst of the Church. 68_marg843: But that we might give ourselves a pattern, etc. It is to be noted that the apostle taught not only by words but exhorted also by deeds. For it belongs to a fit teacher to fulfil in works what he teaches in words. For although it is not unknown that what is taught is true, yet if it begins to be neglected by the teacher, it does not readily profit. For works persuade hearers more than words. And therefore those who profit from words alone, when their teachers are negligent, are to be rewarded with great praise. The apostle, then, was a pattern also to those among the people who were slender in substance, that they might learn not to lose their freedom. Whence also Solomon: “Withdraw thy foot, he says, from the house of thy neighbour, lest having his fill he hate thee.” For he who frequently comes to another’s table, given to idleness, must needs flatter him who feeds him, whereas our religion calls men to freedom.

Some say that the apostle commanded this concerning spiritual works; otherwise, if he spoke of bodily work, in which farmers or craftsmen labour, he would seem to think against the Lord, who says in the Gospel: “Be not solicitous what you shall eat,” etc. But they strive in vain to draw a darkness over themselves and others, so that what charity usefully admonishes they are unwilling not only to do but even to understand, though in many other places of the epistles the apostle most openly teaches what he means here.
